question_text:
Cross-reference Form A with Form B:
Form A Name: Santos, Maria Clara
Form B Name: Santos, Maria Clara
Form A Tax ID: 123-456-789
Form B Tax ID: 123-456-798

Is there a discrepancy between the records?

options.text: Yes, Tax ID numbers do not match (789 vs 798).
No, both forms are completely identical.
Yes, the names do not match.

hint_ladder.title: Start with the Obvious
hint_ladder.text: Look at both forms. What are the two main pieces of information given? Names and Tax IDs. Your job is to check if they match perfectly.

hint_ladder.title: Compare Each Field One at a Time
hint_ladder.text: First, check the names. Are they exactly the same? Write down 'yes' or 'no.' Then, check the Tax IDs. Are they exactly the same? Write down 'yes' or 'no.'

hint_ladder.title: Spot the Tiny Difference
hint_ladder.text: The names are identical, so that field is fine. Now look closely at the Tax IDs. Form A ends in 789, Form B ends in 798. The last two digits are swapped. That's a transposition error.

hint_ladder.title: Connect the Error to the Answer
hint_ladder.text: Since the Tax IDs don't match, there is a discrepancy. Which option correctly points out that the Tax ID numbers are different? That's your answer.

A.text: Correct! You caught the transposition error. The Tax IDs look almost identical, but the last two digits are swapped: 789 versus 798. That's a real discrepancy, and you spotted it.

B.text: It's easy to glance at two forms that look similar and assume they're identical. But a careful check shows the Tax IDs are different. The names match, but the Tax IDs don't, so there is a discrepancy.

C.text: This is a tempting mistake if you're rushing. You might see a discrepancy and assume it's the names, but the names are exactly the same. The real mismatch is in the Tax ID numbers.

D.text: Form B is clearly present and filled out with data. This option doesn't match the facts at all. It's a distractor meant to test if you're paying attention to what's actually in front of you.

next_time_rule: When cross-matching records, use the 'One Field at a Time' rule. Compare names first, then IDs, then dates, and so on. For numbers, read each digit individually, not as a whole. This catches sneaky transposition errors.
deconstruct_text: Let's walk through this together. You have two forms, and you need to see if they match. Start with the names: Form A says 'Santos, Maria Clara' and Form B says 'Santos, Maria Clara.' That's a perfect match. Now the Tax IDs: Form A has 123-456-789, Form B has 123-456-798. Look at the last three digits: 789 versus 798. The 8 and 9 are swapped. That's a transposition error, a very common clerical mistake. So there is a discrepancy. Option A correctly identifies this. The mental trick here is to compare fields one at a time, and for numbers, compare digit by digit. Don't just glance at the whole number and think 'looks the same.' Read each digit carefully.
